newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN DRAW PITS CSKA V CSKA.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN DRAW PITS CSKA V CSKA.

text.p: Russian army side CSKA Moscow face a grudge match, city derby and legal battle rolled into one when they skate out for a Russian Hockey League game in October.
The opposition? CSKA Moscow, of course.

Officials from both teams, who have dragged litigation through the courts for years over the use of one of the biggest names in Russian sport, said on Friday they had no intention of backing down or changing their title after the draw for next season pitted them against each other for the first time.

October 13 will see the first encounter between privately-run Hockey Club CSKA Moscow, led by legendary Soviet coach Viktor Tikhonov, and CSKA Moscow, the defence ministry side which won promotion to the top division this year.
Viktor Zhluktov, manager of the Central Army Sports Club's (CSKA) hockey team, told Reuters that military officials would continue trying to force Tikhonov to stop using the name CSKA.
"We respect Tikhonov as the coach who led the Soviet Union to the heights of hockey. But our patience is running out," he said. "This could only happen in a crazy, lawless country."

Tikhonov, who ran the world-beating Soviet "Big Red Machine" in the 1980s, brought in commercial backers to support the CSKA side he was coaching in 1992 as funds dried up for the Russian army and sport in general following the collapse of communism.
His side still uses the army stadium and facilities.
After falling out with Tikhonov, the army, however, won the right to field their own CSKA hockey team, which, coached by Alexander Volkhov, won promotion from the lower league.
Inna Gushchina, lawyer for Tikhonov's CSKA, called the situation "a Russian paradox" but insisted Tikhonov had more right to the CSKA name.
"We have had this name since 1992 and we do not have to prove to anybody that it is our legal name," she said.
